title: Magnetic Properties of High-Entropy Alloy FeCoNiTi

recollection.starting_material: A high-entropy alloy composed of Iron (Fe), Cobalt (Co), Nickel (Ni), and Titanium (Ti), likely in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios.
recollection.intervention: Synthesis via arc melting or similar high-temperature processing, followed by annealing or rapid solidification, with magnetic characterization (VSM/SQUID) performed at various temperatures.
recollection.structure: A single-phase solid solution (likely FCC or BCC) or a multiphase mixture depending on the Ti content and heat treatment, potentially exhibiting spin-glass or superparamagnetic behavior.
recollection.mechanism: The magnetic properties are governed by the competition between ferromagnetic exchange interactions of Fe, Co, and Ni and the dilution/magnetic moment reduction caused by non-magnetic or weakly magnetic Ti atoms, along with potential spin-glass freezing due to chemical disorder.
recollection.results: The alloy likely exhibits a transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic or spin-glass behavior as Ti content increases, with a Curie temperature significantly lower than that of pure FeCoNi, and a saturation magnetization reduced by approximately 30-50% compared to the FeCoNi baseline. (Note: This is a best guess based on general trends in FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloys, as no specific 2024 paper with this exact title is in my training data.)

score.note: The recollection generically mentions arc melting/rapid solidification, overlapping with the actual rapid-quench synthesis, but omits the composition-matched C14-dominant comparison. It does not identify the specific fcc+C14 dual-phase structure or chemical segregation. The proposed Fe/Co/Ni–Ti competition and moment reduction is broadly related but misses the specific antiferromagnetic sublattice coupling, phase-resolved transitions, orbital contribution, and domain-wall pinning. The guessed 30–50% magnetization reduction is unsupported and omits the reported 1084, 214, and 168 K transitions and 667 Oe coercivity.
